```{r setup}
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
source('../load_release.R');invisible(load_release(normalizePath('..')))
source('report_helpers.R')
r <- readRDS('../generated/report_data.rds')
q <- r$qc[r$qc$passage>0, ]
fmt <- function(x) format(round(x),big.mark=',',trim=TRUE)
treatment_colors <- c('Chloramphenicol'=blue,'No antibiotic'=gold)
show_length_summary <- function(sample) {
  d <- Filter(function(x)identical(x$sample,sample),r$diagnostics)
  stopifnot(length(d)==1)
  s <- d[[1]]$summary
  names(s) <- c('Length_group','Sequences','Reads','Sequence_share','Read_share')
  report_gt(s,'D · Length summary') |>
    gt::cols_label(Length_group='Length group',Sequence_share='Of sequences',Read_share='Of reads') |>
    gt::fmt_integer(columns=c(Sequences,Reads)) |>
    gt::tab_source_note('Sequence share = group sequences / all extracted sequences. Read share = group reads / all extracted reads. Rounded shares may not sum to exactly 100%.')
}
```

## What this analysis establishes

We reconstructed **six bacterial populations**: three grown with a constant low
chloramphenicol concentration and three grown without antibiotic. The selected
time series contain **`r fmt(sum(q$input_reads))` reads across 75 samples**;
barbac extraction retained **`r sprintf('%.2f%%',100*sum(q$extracted_reads)/sum(q$input_reads))`**.
The three shared initial samples add **`r fmt(sum(r$qc$input_reads[r$qc$passage==0]))` reads**.
They are processed once and reused as the baseline for all six populations.

All 75 input-read totals match the corresponding published sample totals exactly.
For the **20 published dominant barcodes in each population**, the median
population-level Spearman rank correlation of final frequencies is **`r sprintf('%.4f',median(r$final_summary$Spearman))`**.
A value near 1 means the two analyses rank these barcodes in a similar order.
The mean absolute difference across the 120 entries is
**`r sprintf('%.3f',100*mean(abs(r$top$barbac_final-r$top$published_final)))` percentage points**
when dividing by all input reads, and
**`r sprintf('%.3f',100*mean(abs(r$top$barbac_final_extracted-r$top$published_final)))` percentage points**
when dividing by extracted barcode reads. Both calculations include absent calls.
This is agreement with published measurements, not an accuracy percentage.

**The publication's final-frequency denominator is unresolved.** One population's
published top-20 frequencies exceed its reported fraction of reads with barcodes.
The report therefore shows both explicit normalizations and the source discrepancy.

The publication provides per-sample summary statistics and average/final
frequencies for its dominant barcodes. Those tables support the numerical checks
shown here. They do not supply the complete author count matrix needed to verify
every reconstructed trajectory or every diversity value.

## The experiment, starting from the beginning

The study asks how bacterial lineages compete during prolonged growth under
different antibiotic regimens. A **lineage** is a family of cells descended from
a labelled ancestor. The researchers inserted a DNA identification tag into the
chromosome, mixed many tagged lineages, and followed their relative abundance
by sequencing the tags at successive passages. The tag identifies a lineage;
its sequence is not itself a measurement of antibiotic resistance.
[Jasinska et al., Nature Ecology & Evolution (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-020-1103-z)

Our selected experiment uses **one barcode per lineage, nominally 15 bases long**.
The original mixture contains many more lineages than could be studied one by
one. We selected two conditions from the constant-concentration experiment:
**chloramphenicol at 1 µg/mL** and **no antibiotic**, both in the same supplemented
M9 medium. A passage is a transfer into fresh growth medium; the authors use
approximately six generations per passage.

```{r experiment-table}
scope <- q |>
  group_by(treatment,population) |>
  summarise(Samples=n(),First_passage=min(passage),Last_passage=max(passage),
    Sequenced_reads=sum(input_reads),.groups='drop')
report_gt(scope,'Selected populations','All deposited timepoints and sequencing subsamples for these populations') |>
  gt::cols_label(treatment='Condition',population='Biological replicate',First_passage='First passage',
    Last_passage='Last passage',Sequenced_reads='Sequenced reads') |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns=c(Samples,First_passage,Last_passage,Sequenced_reads))
```

There are three biological repeats per condition. Each sample was deposited in
four sequencing subsamples; these four files are pooled into one observation.
They do not increase the number of biological replicates. The three initial
population samples are pooled into a shared passage-zero reference.

```{r sampling-timeline}
timeline <- q
timeline$population <- factor(timeline$population,levels=rev(sort(unique(timeline$population))))
p <- ggplot(timeline,aes(passage,population,color=treatment))+
  geom_line(aes(group=population),linewidth=.5)+geom_point(size=2.7)+
  scale_color_manual(values=treatment_colors)+scale_x_continuous(breaks=c(0,2,6,10,14,18,22,30))+
  labs(x='Passage',y=NULL,color=NULL,title='Sampling times for the six populations')+
  barbac::theme_barbac(base_size=12,family='Arial')
report_widget(p,400)
```

Each dot is a sampled timepoint. Connecting segments show the sampling schedule,
not observations between samples. The longest gap is between passages 22 and 30.
The no-antibiotic populations also have a passage-one sample.

## How DNA reads become lineage counts

The workflow is **FASTQ quality checks → minimum base-quality filtering → mapping
to the barcode cassette → barbac extraction → barbac LV clustering → counts over time**.
These are single-end reads; there is no paired-read merging or UMI deduplication.
Every count in this report is a sequencing-read count, not a direct cell count.

The reference contains 15 placeholder bases at the barcode position. Actual
barcodes are extracted from the observed read sequence, preserving variable
lengths. Because these reads begin near the barcode, mapping identifies the
downstream constant sequence and extraction captures the barcode immediately
before it. Our explicitly documented flank rule differs from the authors'
custom alignment rule; the extraction comparison measures that difference.

```{r retention-summary}
ret <- q |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(Samples=n(),Input=sum(input_reads),Quality_passed=sum(quality_passed),
    Mapped=sum(mapped),Extracted=sum(extracted_reads),.groups='drop') |>
  mutate(Retained=Extracted/Input)
report_gt(ret,'Read accounting','Each percentage uses all input reads in the same condition') |>
  gt::cols_label(treatment='Condition',Input='Input reads',Quality_passed='Quality passed',
    Mapped='Mapped reads',Extracted='Extracted barcode reads',Retained='Retained') |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns=c(Samples,Input,Quality_passed,Mapped,Extracted)) |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns=Retained,decimals=2)
```

Reads must have Phred quality at least 10 at every sequenced base. Only primary
alignments enter the mapping count, so supplementary alignments cannot count a
read twice. “Retained” describes extraction yield and does not measure correct
clustering.

```{r mapping-diagnostic}
mapping <- q |> group_by(population) |>
  summarise(mapped=sum(mapped),unmapped=sum(unmapped),.groups='drop') |>
  rename(sample=population)
p <- barbac::plot_bam_stats(mapping)+barbac::theme_barbac(base_size=12,family='Arial')+
  scale_y_continuous(labels=scales::label_number(scale=1e-6,suffix='M'))+
  labs(y='Quality-passed reads',title='Mapping outcomes by biological population')
report_widget(p,450)
```

These bars use barbac's own mapping plot. They partition quality-passed reads
into mapped and unmapped observations. Reads rejected by the quality filter are
already excluded here; the table above retains the original-input denominator.

```{r extraction-comparison}
ex <- r$comparison |> group_by(population) |>
  summarise(Barbac=sum(extracted_reads)/sum(input_reads_barbac),
    Publication=sum(extracted_fraction*input_reads_publication)/sum(input_reads_publication),.groups='drop') |>
  mutate(Difference_pp=100*(Barbac-Publication))
report_gt(ex,'Extraction yield compared with the publication','Weighted by input reads within each population') |>
  gt::cols_label(population='Population',Barbac='Barbac retained',Publication='Published retained',
    Difference_pp='Difference (pp)') |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns=c(Barbac,Publication),decimals=2) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns=Difference_pp,decimals=2) |>
  gt::tab_source_note('The publication reports rounded extraction fractions. A higher yield is not evidence of higher accuracy; the extraction rules differ.')
```

## Extraction diagnostics explained: A, B, C and D

These panels use the existing **`barbac_xtr.stats()`** calculations. They describe
distinct extracted sequences **before clustering**, when several sequences may
still be errors derived from the same lineage. Each sequence contributes once
to each histogram, regardless of its read count.

- **A — Length:** the horizontal axis is barcode length in bases; the vertical
  axis counts distinct sequences. The design length is 15. Dashed lines at 14
  and 16 delimit the near-nominal group used in panel D; they are not extraction
  filters. Extraction accepts 10–20 bases, and the published dominant-barcode
  table itself contains some shorter-than-15 sequences.
- **B — Abundance:** how many sequences have each read count. On the log₁₀ axis,
  0 means one read, 1 means ten reads, and 2 means one hundred reads.
- **C — Base-composition entropy:** how evenly A, C, G and T occur within an
  individual sequence. `AAAA` has 0 bits; `ACGT` has 2 bits. This measure ignores
  base order: a repetitive `ACGTACGT` also has 2 bits. It is not a direct score
  of sequence randomness, sequencing accuracy, or population diversity.
- **D — Length summary:** a native `gt` table. “Sequences” counts distinct DNA
  strings; “Reads” sums their observations. The two percentage columns therefore
  have different denominators, explicitly named in the footnote.

Expand a population/timepoint below. Early and final samples are shown for all
six populations. The complete sample statistics are available in the accompanying
[extraction summary CSV](../results/extraction_summary.csv).

::: {.note}
**Three different uses of “entropy”.**
Panel C measures base composition within one barcode, in bits. The paper's
Extended Data Figure 1 instead measures nucleotide variation across the barcode
library at each sequence position, using natural logarithms. The population
diversity plots below use abundances of whole lineages. These measurements answer
different questions and must not be compared as though they were the same score.
:::

## Following the mixture over time

The following plots show the same four barcode identities in every panel, chosen
from the authors' dominant-barcode table using summed published mean frequencies
across the six selected populations. Their colours stay fixed. A barcode label is
its DNA identifier, not a treatment name or an inferred mutation.

Read the **thickness of a coloured band** as that group's fraction of all reads.
**All remaining barcodes** adds together every extracted lineage other than the
four displayed separately. **No extracted barcode** represents input reads without
an accepted extracted barcode. These groups are kept separate, and every vertical
slice adds to 100%. Neither group is automatically classified as sequencing errors.
This is our explicit read-accounting denominator. The denominator used for the
publication's final-frequency table is examined separately below.

::: {.panel-tabset}
### Chloramphenicol · replicate 1
```{r composition-c1}
r$composition[['Low CMP r1']]
```
### Chloramphenicol · replicate 2
```{r composition-c2}
r$composition[['Low CMP r2']]
```

```{r composition-c3}
r$composition[['Low CMP r3']]
```
### No antibiotic · replicate 1
```{r composition-n1}
r$composition[['No drug r1']]
```
### No antibiotic · replicate 2
```{r composition-n2}
r$composition[['No drug r2']]
```
### No antibiotic · replicate 3
```{r composition-n3}
r$composition[['No drug r3']]
```
:::

Hover to identify a band. The areas interpolate between measured passages; they
do not imply observations at every intervening generation. A rise means an
increasing share of measured reads. Inferring resistance or assigning a causal
mutation would require additional evidence.

## Diversity asks how many lineages contribute

All diversity calculations use the **complete lineage counts**, before any
display grouping into “All remaining barcodes”. The three panels answer different
questions: how many lineages are detected; how many equally abundant lineages
would give the observed Shannon diversity; and how strongly one lineage dominates.
For example, four equally abundant lineages give a value of four for all three.
In the bottom panel, a value of 2 means the largest lineage accounts for half
the extracted barcode reads; a value near 1 means one lineage dominates.

For this constant-concentration experiment, the authors reported faster loss of
lineage diversity under low chloramphenicol than in the other conditions
(Extended Data Figure 6). The comparison here focuses on chloramphenicol and the
untreated control. It can check that contrast, while all three replicates remain
visible. [Study, constant-drug results](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-020-1103-z)

```{r diversity}
long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(r$diversity,
  c(richness,assigned_shannon_effective,assigned_inverse_dominance),names_to='metric',values_to='value')
long$metric <- factor(long$metric,levels=c('richness','assigned_shannon_effective','assigned_inverse_dominance'),
  labels=c('Detected lineages','Effective lineages · Shannon','Inverse dominant-lineage share'))
p <- ggplot(long,aes(passage,value,color=treatment,group=population,
    text=paste(population,'· passage',passage)))+
  geom_line(aes(linetype=factor(replicate)),linewidth=.7)+geom_point(size=1.5)+
  facet_wrap(~metric,ncol=1,scales='free_y')+scale_y_log10(labels=scales::label_number(big.mark=','))+
  scale_color_manual(values=treatment_colors)+
  labs(x='Passage',y='Number / effective number (log scale)',color=NULL,linetype='Replicate',
    title='Lineage diversity through time')+barbac::theme_barbac(base_size=12,family='Arial')
report_widget(p,800)
```

```{r diversity-findings}
end_cmp <- r$diversity$assigned_shannon_effective[r$diversity$passage==30 & r$diversity$treatment=='Chloramphenicol']
end_control <- r$diversity$assigned_shannon_effective[r$diversity$passage==30 & r$diversity$treatment=='No antibiotic']
stopifnot(length(end_cmp)==3,length(end_control)==3)
shared <- r$diversity |> filter(passage>0) |> group_by(passage,treatment) |>
  summarise(effective=median(assigned_shannon_effective),.groups='drop') |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from=treatment,values_from=effective)
shared <- shared[complete.cases(shared),]
```

At passage 30, the median Shannon effective number is
**`r sprintf('%.1f',median(end_cmp))` lineages with chloramphenicol** and
**`r sprintf('%.1f',median(end_control))` without antibiotic**. Across
**`r sum(shared[['Chloramphenicol']]<shared[['No antibiotic']])` of `r nrow(shared)`**
matched sampled passages, the chloramphenicol populations have the lower median.
This describes the contrast in the reconstructed observations. It is not a
formal test of the rate of diversity loss or a replication of all the authors'
diversity calculations.

Replicates differ substantially: at passage 30, the chloramphenicol values range
from **`r sprintf('%.1f',min(end_cmp))` to `r sprintf('%.1f',max(end_cmp))`**, and
the untreated values range from **`r sprintf('%.1f',min(end_control))` to
`r sprintf('%.1f',max(end_control))`**. The median contrast does not mean that every
treated population has lower diversity than every untreated population.

For the effective-number panels, frequencies are normalized **among extracted
barcode reads**, so they describe the observed lineage mixture. The exported data
also contain calculations using all input reads as an alternative denominator.
Sequencing depth and extraction yield affect detection of rare lineages, so a
lower richness value alone is not proof of biological extinction. The shared
initial sample does not provide six independent baseline observations.
Because clustering is performed separately for each pooled population, its
assignments of the shared initial reads can differ. Differences between
passage-zero diversity values therefore do not represent different starting
biological populations.

```{r cluster-summary}
cs <- r$diversity |> filter(passage %in% c(2,30)) |>
  select(population,passage,n_clusters,n_singletons,largest_cluster_frac,top10_frac)
report_gt(cs,'Cluster summaries at matched early and final passages',
  'Calculated with barbac::cluster_stats() after reconstructing each sample') |>
  gt::cols_label(population='Population',passage='Passage',n_clusters='Detected lineages',
    n_singletons='One-read lineages',largest_cluster_frac='Largest lineage',top10_frac='Top 10 lineages') |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns=c(passage,n_clusters,n_singletons)) |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns=c(largest_cluster_frac,top10_frac),decimals=2) |>
  gt::tab_source_note('The last two columns are shares of extracted barcode reads. One-read lineages are detected clusters supported by one read in this sample. Their count is not a false-positive count.')
```

The last two columns show concentration of the observed population: a larger
share held by one or ten lineages means fewer lineages dominate the read counts.
Passages 2 and 30 are available in every selected population. Rare lineages can
be missed at finite sequencing depth, so absence of reads is not proof of absence
of cells.

## What agrees with the published measurements?

The strongest available numerical checks are the sample statistics in
Supplementary Table 1c and the 20 dominant-barcode entries per population in
Supplementary Table 4b. We use the **same treatment, replicate and passage** for
each comparison. The comparison includes all 120 selected population/barcode
entries, including the shorter barcode reported for one untreated replicate.

There is a source discrepancy to resolve before calling the final frequencies
an exact reproduction. For **Low CMP r1 at passage 30**, Table 4b's 20 final
frequencies sum to **86.94%**, while Table 1c reports barcode extraction from
**80.24%** of input reads. If both use all input reads, the subset of 20 lineages
cannot exceed the total fraction with identified barcodes. The difference is
far larger than rounding. Different denominators or a mismatch between the
published tables could explain it; the supplied material does not resolve which.

```{r denominator-audit}
audit <- r$denominator_audit |>
  mutate(Interpretation=ifelse(Incompatible_with_all_input,'Cannot reconcile','Not ruled out')) |>
  select(Population,Published_top20_sum,Published_extracted_fraction,Interpretation)
report_gt(audit,'Can the published final frequencies use all input reads?',
  'A consistency check between Supplementary Tables 4b and 1c') |>
  gt::cols_label(Published_top20_sum='Top-20 frequencies summed',
    Published_extracted_fraction='All reads with identified barcodes',Interpretation='All-input interpretation') |>
  gt::fmt_percent(columns=c(Published_top20_sum,Published_extracted_fraction),decimals=2) |>
  gt::tab_source_note('Not ruled out does not establish the denominator. The check allows for rounding of the extraction fraction.')
```

```{r richness-comparison}
x <- merge(r$diversity[r$diversity$passage>0,],r$comparison[c('population','passage','clustered_sequences')],
  by=c('population','passage'))
long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(x,c(richness,clustered_sequences),names_to='Source',values_to='Lineages')
long$Source <- factor(long$Source,levels=c('richness','clustered_sequences'),labels=c('Barbac LV','Publication'))
p <- ggplot(long,aes(passage,Lineages,color=Source,linetype=Source))+
  geom_line()+geom_point(size=1.4)+facet_wrap(~population,ncol=2)+scale_y_log10(labels=scales::label_number(big.mark=','))+
  scale_color_manual(values=c('Barbac LV'=blue,'Publication'='#6B6B6B'))+
  labs(x='Passage',y='Detected lineages (log scale)',title='Reported and reconstructed lineage richness')+
  barbac::theme_barbac(base_size=11,family='Arial')
report_widget(p,750)
```

Solid and dashed lines compare the number of detected lineages. Differences can
come from extraction rules and clustering, including different treatment of rare
sequences. Fewer clusters do not by themselves establish better correction.

```{r final-frequencies}
x <- tidyr::pivot_longer(r$top,c(barbac_final,barbac_final_extracted),
  names_to='Normalization',values_to='Barbac_frequency')
x$Normalization <- factor(x$Normalization,levels=c('barbac_final','barbac_final_extracted'),
  labels=c('All input reads','Extracted barcode reads'))
p <- ggplot(x,aes(100*published_final,100*Barbac_frequency,color=Normalization,
    text=paste(population,barcode)))+
  geom_abline(slope=1,intercept=0,color='#6B6B6B',linetype=2)+
  geom_point(alpha=.7,size=2)+facet_wrap(~population,ncol=2,scales='free')+
  scale_color_manual(values=c('All input reads'=blue,'Extracted barcode reads'=gold))+
  labs(x='Published final frequency (%)',y='Barbac final frequency (%)',
    title='Final frequencies under two explicit normalizations',color='Barbac denominator')+
  barbac::theme_barbac(base_size=11,family='Arial')
report_widget(p,750)
```

Each barcode has two points at the last sampled passage, corresponding to the
two barbac denominators. Published values are plotted as provided; their
denominator remains unresolved. The dashed line indicates equal numeric
frequencies. A barcode absent under its exact published identifier is assigned
zero in both versions and retained in every calculation.
For example, a published frequency of 10% and a barbac frequency of 9% differ
by **one percentage point**.

```{r agreement-table}
report_gt(select(r$final_summary,Population,Published_barcodes,Spearman,
    Mean_absolute_difference_input_pp,Mean_absolute_difference_extracted_pp),
  'Final-frequency comparison with both denominators','Twenty published barcode entries per population') |>
  gt::cols_label(Published_barcodes='Barcodes',Mean_absolute_difference_input_pp='Mean absolute difference: all input (pp)',
    Mean_absolute_difference_extracted_pp='Mean absolute difference: extracted (pp)') |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns=Spearman,decimals=4) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns=c(Mean_absolute_difference_input_pp,Mean_absolute_difference_extracted_pp),decimals=3) |>
  gt::tab_source_note('pp = percentage points. Spearman measures rank agreement and is unchanged by positive rescaling within a population. It is not an accuracy percentage. The source discrepancy prevents attributing all absolute differences to clustering.')
```

The selected barcodes were defined by the publication, not chosen because barbac
agreed with them. They are abundant lineages, so these checks do not establish
accuracy for the much larger set of rare lineages. Author mean frequencies are
also retained in the exported table; we do not claim exact agreement of means
without resolving the denominator, initial-timepoint and averaging conventions.

## Inspect the observations behind the plots

Search by population, barcode or passage. Both barbac denominators are available.
“Published final” is populated only at
the final passage because a full published per-timepoint count matrix was not
available in the supplementary tables. Blank reference entries mean unavailable
reference measurements, not zero abundance.

## Processing time and interpretation limits

```{r timing}
report_gt(r$times,'Barbac LV clustering time','One pooled trajectory reconstruction per population') |>
  gt::cols_label(population='Population',unique_input_sequences='Input sequences',clusters='Pooled clusters',
    clustering_seconds='Elapsed (s)',clustering_cpu_seconds='CPU time (s)',input_read_observations='Pooled read observations') |>
  gt::fmt_integer(columns=c(unique_input_sequences,clusters,input_read_observations)) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns=c(clustering_seconds,clustering_cpu_seconds),decimals=2) |>
  gt::tab_source_note(paste0('Times cover the optimized release clustering call, including support ordering, with up to ',r$release$workers,' concurrent release-clustering processes. Recorded R platform: ',r$release$build$platform,'. Elapsed time includes scheduling; CPU time reports active process computation. Download, quality checks, mapping, extraction and report generation are excluded. Each population includes the shared baseline once; pooled read totals must not be summed as unique sequencing input.'))
```

The release package was compiled with optimization enabled. Its complete
compiler command and binary hash are saved with the timing validation.

```{r timing-provenance, results='asis'}
reruns <- sum(grepl('^Release rerun:',unlist(r$release$populations,use.names=FALSE)))
if(reruns>0)cat(sprintf('%d complete release reruns were compared with existing clustering results. Every barcode assignment and centroid count matched exactly.\n\n',reruns))
if(reruns<nrow(r$times))cat('The remaining timings came from original clustering runs using the same verified release binary.\n\n')
```

The [result notes](../results/README.md) record the hardware and concurrent work
for the checked-in local measurements, including the earlier unoptimized
development timings archived separately from the release table.

Clustering uses barbac LV at distance 3, support ordering, merge ratio 20 and the
Poisson indel option, with an assumed error rate of 0.005. These settings were
fixed before evaluating publication agreement. Each population is pooled over
its timepoints with the shared initial population, so reconstruction uses future
samples retrospectively. It is not a prospective prediction.

Distance 3 allows candidate barcodes to differ by up to three insertions,
deletions or substitutions. The assumed 0.005 error rate (0.5% per base) is a
separate parameter used when scoring possible parents; it is not estimated from
the publication-agreement percentage. Abundance guards also constrain merging,
so being within three edits does not automatically put two barcodes together.

This analysis uses build **`r r$provenance$build`**. An exact search optimization
skips wider-search parents that cannot satisfy the existing abundance guard,
after all distance-one candidates have been examined. The old and new builds
give identical assignments on a 12,000-sequence real-data check, and indexed
search agrees with exhaustive scans in the regression tests. The scoring and
merge rules are unchanged. These application timings are not a replacement for
the separate controlled method benchmark.

This report tests whether barbac reconstructs the selected study measurements.
It does not establish the correctness of every barcode assignment, identify causal
mutations, or reproduce the paper's entire analysis. Complete author count tables
and alignment code would allow a more exact reconciliation of extraction,
individual trajectories and diversity. The published methods state that their
custom analysis scripts are available on request; no request has been sent.
False-positive and false-negative counts require known true labels; the
publication's processed output is not such a truth set.

## Sources and reproducibility

- [Study and Methods](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-020-1103-z): experimental
  design, barcode construct, processing conventions and biological interpretation.
- [BioProject PRJNA592529](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/bioproject/PRJNA592529):
  raw reads from the constant-concentration experiment. The accompanying sample
  manifests record every selected run and its checksum.
- [Author supplementary tables](https://media.springernature.com/original/springer-static/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41559-020-1103-z/MediaObjects/41559_2020_1103_MOESM3_ESM.xlsx):
  Table 1c supplies sample totals and processing summaries; Table 4b supplies
  dominant barcode identities and mean/final frequencies.

The accompanying analysis folder contains the R scripts, cassette FASTA,
checksum receipts, complete reconstructed count matrices and a SLURM script.
The report embeds its figures and interactive tables for offline viewing.
The SLURM script is prepared for reuse and has not been submitted to a cluster.
